column4: The 1820 Alabama legislative manumission act (Acts, Nov. 1820, p.62, approved Dec. 11, 1820; DB1 row 176) authorized John N.S. Jones and Alexander P. Shandy's age (3 in Dec. 1820) matches Shandy Wesley Jones's well-documented birth date of Dec. 20, 1816 in Huntsville, Madison Co., AL. All independent sources agree: born enslaved in Huntsville/Madison Co. AL 1816, emancipated as a young child, moved to Tuscaloosa before age 21, married Evalina Love in 1837, became a prosperous barber and real estate investor, served in the Alabama House of Representatives 1868-1870 (Tuscaloosa's first Black elected official), fled KKK violence to Moundville then Mobile in 1871, appointed to U.S. Customs House by President Grant, pastored Little Zion/Big Zion AME Zion Church, died Feb. 4, 1886, buried Magnolia Cemetery Mobile. column4: Secondary source (Huntsville History Collection article, already in DB1 rows 55/169) states Llewellen Jones "came to north Alabama at about the same time as" the Broad River Group and "was part of the 'Georgia Faction'" at the 1809 Huntsville land sale, though "apparently had no political aspirations for himself." Broad River Group leaders (Pope, Bibb, Walker, Tait) founded Huntsville, its bank, and dominated early Alabama politics. JNS Jones was a prominent Huntsville attorney in the same era (1819 Constitutional Convention period), whose law office housed Alabama's first public library. (2026-08-03 update: I ran two independent research passes -- a dedicated Broad River Group research review, and a direct Ancestry profile check of both Llewellen Jones and John N.S. Jones -- and found no documented Georgia [Wilkes/Elbert Co.] residency for either man. Their documented path runs Virginia straight to Alabama, with a Nashville stop for J.N.S. Jones's 1821 marriage. I still have their contemporaneous presence in the same 1809 Huntsville land-sale wave as the Broad River figures documented, but that's the only confirmed connection I've got so far.) I confirmed the Broad River Group is a real, formally named historiographical term, not just a description I made up or that the Huntsville History Collection article implied loosely: it was coined by historian J. Mills Thornton III in his 1978 book 'Politics and Power in a Slave Society: Alabama, 1800-1860' (Louisiana State University Press). The group's origin: in 1784, Gen. George Mathews led Revolutionary War veterans from the Charlottesville, Virginia area to settle along the Broad River in north Georgia, near Petersburg, GA. This group intermarried with existing planter families and became wealthy tobacco/cotton planters, sometimes called the 'Georgia Faction' in Alabama sources -- the exact phrase used in the Huntsville History Collection's Jones-family article. When the federal government opened land around future Huntsville, Broad River investors -- led by LeRoy Pope, John Williams Walker (also a Virginia native, born Amelia County, whose father migrated Amelia Co., VA -> Wilkes Co., GA in 1783), and future governor Thomas Bibb -- bought roughly half the land sold at the 1809 Huntsville public auction. This confirms the Broad River Group is the same migration pattern I've been asking about, and it directly supports treating Llewellen Jones's VA-to-AL migration as historical scaffolding/context, even though I still haven't found a personal or business tie linking him by name to Pope, Bibb, or Walker specifically. [2026-08-04, round 2 targeted follow-up] I did a dedicated follow-up pass this round specifically to check whether our Jones family was really part of the Broad River Group. I confirmed 'Broad River Group' and 'Georgia Faction' are the same historical network -- Chase Tate's Huntsville Historical Review article uses both terms interchangeably (https://huntsvillehistorycollection.org/hhc/docs/pdf/hhr/Volume_39_2_Fall-Winter-14.pdf?a=hhr). But the important nuance: Tate's article names our Llewellen Jones on page 66 ONLY as 'one Huntsville citizen' who hanged himself during the Panic of 1819 -- NOT explicitly as a Broad River Group member. Tate's footnote there cites Daniel Dupre's 'Transforming the Cotton Frontier: Madison County, Alabama, 1800-1840' (LSU Press, 1997), pp.6-7, 57, 62 -- I have NOT examined Dupre's book yet, and it's now my highest-priority unread source (see DB3 new row for Dupre). I also checked E. Merton Coulter's 'Old Petersburg and the Broad River Valley of Georgia' index directly and found ZERO entries for Llewellyn/Lewellen Jones, Spotswood, Perkins, or Scruggs. So Jacquelyn Gray's article remains the ONLY source I've found asserting our Jones family was part of the Broad River Group/Georgia Faction.

[2026-08-04, pass 4 -- STRENGTHENING PRIMARY-SOURCE EVIDENCE] I confirmed directly against the primary source at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (enrolled 1820 legislative act, "An act to authorize John N. S. Jones and Alexander P. Jones to emancipate certain slaves therein named," approved Dec. 11, 1820, ADAH Voices of Alabama collection, item 9761: https://digital.archives.alabama.gov/digital/collection/voices/id/9761/ ; full 2-page zoom viewer: https://digital.archives.alabama.gov/digital/pdf.js/web/viewer.html?file=/digital/api/collection/voices/id/9761/download#page=1&zoom=auto,-96,1269, file ref Q110258-Q110259) that this act is dated December 11, 1820 -- just 9 months after Llewellyn Jones's death on March 6, 1820. Both of his sons, John N.S. Jones and Alexander P. Jones, jointly petitioned to free Elizabeth (40), Evalina (13), Ann (6), and Shandy (3) almost immediately after inheriting/settling their father's estate. This timing is consistent with an inheritance-driven manumission rather than a routine sale-related freeing, which I think meaningfully strengthens this hypothesis. I am NOT treating this as confirmed proof of paternity or of any blood relationship -- the act itself does not state a family relationship between Elizabeth/Evalina/Ann/Shandy and the Jones family, and this remains a strengthened hypothesis only, not a settled fact. This also newly identifies Elizabeth (age 40 in 1820, b. ~1780) as very likely the mother of Evalina/Ann/Shandy per the document's grouping and ages, though the act does not explicitly state that relationship either -- logged as her own entry at DB2 row 76. [2026-08-04, pass 5 -- MY OWN TREE + NAMING-COLLISION CAUTIONS] I went back into my own Ancestry tree ("Jones Family (Avalon Plantation)," Tree ID 210795668) and found that Maria Louisa (Jones) Donnell's own tree profile lists her parents as John Nelson Spotswood Jones Esq. (1793-1855) and "Elizabeth (Enslaved) Jones," and that a woman recorded in my tree as "Elizabeth (Enslaved) Jones" (no birth/death dates given on this particular profile) is listed as spouse/partner of Llewellyn Jones AND as mother of Maria Louisa (Jones) Donnell, Paul Llewellyn Jones, Walter Blackstone Jones, John Haywood Jones, Marcella Almira Dearing, Ann Jones (b. 1813), and Elizabeth/Evalina Jones (b. 1807) -- profile https://www.ancestry.com/family-tree/person/tree/210795668/person/302764465198/facts. I want to be very explicit that THIS IS UNVERIFIED TREE DATA FROM MY OWN ANCESTRY TREE, found in my own tree's user-contributed profile fields, NOT a confirmed primary source -- I have not yet opened this specific profile to check what documents (if any) are actually cited for these spousal/parental edges, and it may reflect my own prior guesswork, another user's tree hint, or simple tree conflation/error. I also noticed the tree is internally inconsistent here: one profile lists this Elizabeth's partner as "Llewellyn Jones" while another lists Maria's father as "John Nelson Spotswood Jones Esq." (Llewellyn's son) -- this could mean generational confusion/error in the tree, OR that an Elizabeth was connected to both father and son at different points, OR a plain data-entry mistake. I am flagging this inconsistency, not resolving it. IF accurate, this tree entry would mean Paul Llewellyn Jones, Walter Blackstone Jones, John Haywood Jones, Marcella Almira Dearing, and Maria Louisa (Jones) Donnell -- the exact heirs named in the A.P. Jones probate file -- share a mother, an enslaved woman named Elizabeth, with Ann Jones (b.1813) and Elizabeth/Evalina Jones (b.1807), names that closely echo the four people freed in the 1820 emancipation act (Elizabeth 40, Evalina 13, Ann 6, Shandy 3, see row above and DB2 row 76). This could be strong corroborating evidence for this half-sibling hypothesis, OR it could simply be an artifact of tree error/conflation -- I cannot tell which until I check whether these specific tree relationship-edges have actual attached source citations. ACTION ITEM for me, not yet done: open the "Elizabeth (Enslaved) Jones" profile (302764465198) directly and check its source citations before treating any of this as evidence. Huntsville, Madison Co., AL) whose father is recorded as Turner Moore (1780-1867) -- a completely different lineage from the "Alexander P. Jones" I have been tracking throughout this database as Llewellyn Jones's son and the central figure of the A.P. Jones estate probate. There is also a separate "Alexander Thomas Jones" (1834-1857, son of John N.S. Jones) in the white line. This means there may be TWO OR THREE different "Alexander (P.) Jones" individuals in Madison County across the white slaveholding line and the formerly-enslaved-family line who took the Jones surname -- a real risk of research/logging confusion going forward. I am flagging this prominently so that I (and any future logging pass) do not conflate them. This is a DIFFERENT woman from the "Elizabeth (Enslaved) Jones" (spouse/partner of Llewellyn/John N.S. Jones, no dates given, profile 302764465198) described earlier in this note, and BOTH are distinct from "Elizabeth" of the 1820 emancipation act (age 40, DB2 row 76, no tree profile). My tree therefore has AT LEAST THREE separate "Elizabeth"s connected to enslavement and the Jones surname. I am tracking these as three distinct individuals pending further verification and will not merge them without direct source evidence.

Jones v. Perkins, 1 Stewart 512-514: Richard Perkins brought trespass to try title in Madison County Circuit Court against Alexander P. Jones for an undivided third of a tract, claiming under a deed from Benjamin Perkins (who claimed a life estate as husband of, and in right of, his wife — a daughter of Lewellen Jones, entitled to one third of his estate). The court states: 'the premises sued for are a part of the estate of Lewellen Jones, deceased; that the said deceased left two sons, Alexander P. [Jones] the defendant below, John N. S. Jones, and Mrs Perkins, the wife of Benjamin Perkins, his heirs at law.' Alexander offered to prove Benjamin's title had vested by sheriff's sale in Thomas Moore, a judgment creditor of Benjamin, before the sale to Richard Perkins — rejected below. Held: reversed and remanded — the defendant, as heir at law (tenant in the nature of a coparcener, not a mere trespasser), could defeat the plaintiff by proving paramount title in a stranger; one tenant in common cannot maintain trespass to try titles against a co-tenant without proving actual ouster. Counsel: Clay and McClung for the plaintiff in error; Kelly and Hutchinson for the defendant. Judge Saffold not sitting; opinion by the Chief Justice. CORRECTION: the opinion does NOT mention the 1820 manumission of Elizabeth or any enslaved person — it is a land-title dispute among Lewellen Jones's heirs. The timeline's characterization of it as 'a case over the title of the 1820 manumission' should be corrected.

Content: 'DEPOSITION IN REGARD TO THE SHUTTING OUT,' May 31, 1705 — Orlando Jones, 'formerly usher of the Grammar school in William and Mary College,' declares that the custom of 'shutting out the Master' began in 1699 (with no intermission while he belonged to the College except in 1700, when the Assembly obtained leave to dismiss the scholars early), that 'in the year 1702 I went to England & so knew nothing of what Mr. Blair taxes his excellency with, as done in the sd year with a Design of killing or hurting Mr. Blair,' and that from the beginning of the custom there was no design of doing Mr. Blair any hurt or prejudice. Signed 'ORLANDO JONES,' sworn May 31, 1705 before John Smith and John Lewis. Full citation: 'Papers Relating to the Administration of Governor Nicholson and to the Founding of William and Mary College (Continued),' Virginia Magazine of History and Biography, Vol. 8 (1900), pp. 260–261. Orlando Jones (born December 31, 1681; died June 12, 1719), son of Rev. Rowland Jones, usher at the William & Mary grammar school 1700–1702, later burgess for King William County; grandfather (through daughter Frances, m. John Dandridge) of Martha Washington. Firsthand read of Jones v. Fort, 36 Ala. 449 (June Term 1860; appeal from Dallas Circuit Court, Hon. Nat. Cook): Rachel M. Jones (Dallas County) sued Elias W. Fort and Gabriel H. Fort in trover for the loss of an enslaved man named Orange, whom she had hired to her son-in-law Squire Lowry for 1858; on Dec 24, 1858 Lowry's sons loaned Orange to the Forts to help raise a gin-house about a half-mile from Lowry's plantation (itself ~16 miles from Marion); a timber fell and killed him. Held: a hirer's gratuitous loan of a hired slave to another for gin-house raising makes the sub-bailee liable to the owner in trover for the slave's value, no matter what care was exercised. column2: Did Gross Scruggs Sr. marry 'the widow Jones' after Sept 1832 — and is she Mary Anderson Jones?
column5: Resolved — negative finding: the 'widow Jones' was NOT Mary Anderson Jones. She was MARY SAUNDERS, widow of Major William Jones (1779–1832) of Campbell County, VA — son of William Richard Jones (1745–1781, killed at Guilford Courthouse) and Agness Walker (1749–1798), grandson of John and Elizabeth Walker Jones of Buckingham County, VA; married c.1798/99; seven children survived. After Major Jones's death in 1832 she married Gross Scruggs in Madison County, AL in 1833 — his third wife (after Mary 'Polly' Tate, d. Sept 19, 1832); the Scruggs genealogy also notes she was his fourth marriage's predecessor to 'the widow Shotwell.' Evidence per Ethel Hastings Scruggs Dunklin, The Scruggs Genealogy (1912), via a genealogy.com forum post for John Rison Jones: (1) Gross Scruggs Jr. (b. VA 1796, son of Gross + Nancy Logwood) married Mary Susan Saunders of Tennessee, 'a niece of his step-mother'; (2) Mary Saunders Jones Scruggs d. 1850, will written 1845 witnessed by her nephew William T. Saunders, leaving Saunders silver (6 teaspoons, 6 tablespoons) to son James S. Jones (1800–1853). The Joneses and Scruggses were both Buckingham/Bedford/Campbell VA families, came to Alabama in 1818, and were close neighbors in Madison County. Primary targets: Mary's 1845 will; the Sept 1833 marriage return (Madison Co. Marriage Records v.A — FamilySearch gated).
